name: Monterrey International Airport
before:
Mexico's fourth busiest airport by passenger numbers, and growing quickly: 15.6 million passengers in 2025, up from 13.6 million the year before. It serves Greater Monterrey from Apodaca in Nuevo León, sits at 390 metres above sea level and works as the main hub for Viva, Magnicharters and Aerus, with Volaris treating it as a focus city.

The route map is wider than the domestic traffic suggests, reaching across Mexico and the Americas and out to Asia and Europe. Two runways handle it. The primary, 11/29, is 3,000 metres long with an ILS approach, and a shorter second runway at 1,800 metres takes lighter aircraft.

Alongside the scheduled airlines it carries flight training, general aviation and the national airspace navigation service, so the apron is busier and more mixed than at a purely commercial field. It is operated by Grupo Aeroportuario Centro Norte and named after Mariano Escobedo, a nineteenth century general from the state.
after:
Monterrey's airport handled 15.6 million passengers in 2025, up 15 per cent on 13.6 million the year before. It serves Greater Monterrey from Apodaca in Nuevo León, sits at 390 metres above sea level and is the main hub for Viva. Volaris also flies here, as does the regional airline Aerus.

The route map reaches across Mexico and the rest of the Americas and out to Asia and Europe. Two runways handle it: the main one is 3,000 metres long and the second 1,800 metres.

It also handles general aviation, and is operated by Grupo Aeroportuario del Centro Norte (OMA).

claims.wasBefore: Mexico's fourth busiest airport by passenger numbers
claims.why: Wikipedia alone. AFAC's national table on gob.mx answers with an Akamai challenge page and OMA's investor site (ir.oma.aero) with a SiteGround CAPTCHA; OMA's own releases give Monterrey's total but no national rank. The operators' 2025 totals put Monterrey (15.6 million) behind Guadalajara (18.7 million, GAP) and ahead of Tijuana (12.65 million, GAP), with Cancún second (ASUR, citing AFAC), but the Mexico City airports' figures could not be read to close the ranking.
Replaced by the growth figure itself: up 15.0 per cent in 2025 (OMA).

claims.claim: main hub for Magnicharters and Aerus
claims.why: Magnicharters is not on OMA's current list of the airport's airlines, so it goes. Aerus is kept as flying from here (OMA, March 2026); 'main hub' for Aerus is Wikipedia's word only.

claims.wasBefore: with Volaris treating it as a focus city
claims.why: 'Focus city' is Wikipedia's label only; softened to 'Volaris also flies here', from OMA's live airline list.

claims.claim: route map wider than the domestic traffic suggests
claims.wasBefore: The route map is wider than the domestic traffic suggests
claims.why: Framing, dropped for a plain statement of where the routes go. Domestic passengers were 13.1 of the 15.6 million in 2025 (OMA).
Sources disagree on the designator: Wikipedia's text says 11/29, its infobox and OurAirports say 12/30. The length is kept.
Not what the sources say: Wikipedia calls the second runway seldom used, and OMA says only that it can take some compatible aircraft while the main runway is resurfaced (held back below).
Wikipedia alone. General aviation is kept (OMA).
Wikipedia alone. SENEAM's own page is on gob.mx, which answers with an Akamai challenge page; not tried again.

claims.claim: named after Mariano Escobedo, a nineteenth century general from the state
claims.wasBefore: named after Mariano Escobedo, a nineteenth century general from the state
claims.why: The naming rests on Wikipedia alone: OMA's pages call it Monterrey International Airport, and OurAirports' 'General Mariano Escobedo' keyword sits beside a Wikipedia link, so it is not independent. The encyclopedia confirms Escobedo was a 19th-century Mexican army commander born in Galeana, Nuevo León, but not the naming. Restore it when a second source for the official name (OMA's annual report or Mexico's AIP) can be read.

claims.claim: main runway resurfacing, September to December 2026
claims.why: Held back: OMA is resurfacing the 3,000 m main runway between September and December 2026, mostly overnight, with the auxiliary runway taking some compatible aircraft meanwhile (OMA, 24 June 2026). One source, and a fact the old text has nothing to replace; worth a line for Andy while the works run, as an attributed statement.

claims.claim: terminal expansion under way; nothing new opened
claims.why: Held back: the airport has three terminals, A, B and C, linked by a free shuttle (Wikipedia). OMA is spending MX$8 billion on it in 2026 to 2030; a new three-gate lounge in Terminal A and a broader terminal expansion are under way, due over the coming years, and a light rail terminal is due by the end of 2026 (Mexico Business News, 6 April 2026). No new terminal has opened. The old text says nothing about terminals.
